cognate: ON vaxa ~ Gk ἀέξω ~ Ved. vakṣ-/ukṣ- (*h2weks- 'grow, increase'), the verb of the collocation
drift_or_renewal: the strength noun is renewed in each branch: ON megin/ásmegin, afl; Gk μένος (θυμός, later κάρτος); Ved. śávas (instr.). Gk ἀέξω is transitive here (wine makes it grow), ON vaxa intransitive with strength as subject, but Greek has the intransitive too (θυμὸς ἀέξεται, Od. 2.315)
shared_syntax: *h2weks- + 'strength/fighting spirit' + dative of the hero whose strength it is (ON honum vex ásmegin / honum hafði afl vaxit; Gk ἀνδρὶ ... μένος ἀέξει, μοι ἀέξεται θυμός)
context: a fighter's strength swells beyond its normal measure through an outside agent: Thor's belt (megingjǫrð), so that his ásmegin grows by half; Fenrir's strength having grown; in Homer, wine for a weary warrior; in the RV, Indra growing (vavakṣitha) in each soma-intoxication, made to grow by the drunk soma (pītā́ḥ ukṣayanta)
phrase: *h2weks- + 'strength' (+ dat. of person): 'strength grows in/for the hero'
note: Low: 'strength grows' is natural phrasing, and inheriting the verb (cf. Eng. wax) may be enough to explain it. The heroic-augmentation context, which Homer and the RV share through drink, is the most specific part. Snorri is a learned 13th-c. prose source; the skaldic megin vaxa (AM-242-fol 53:10) is the older witness.

near_miss.lead: maðr ok kona ~ мужи ... женою; svaf ~ спять ('man and woman', sleep)
near_miss.why_not: Not the same context (Ymir sweating out a man and a woman under his left arm, against the Chronicle's Britons with many men sleeping with one wife). Only kona ~ жена is a clean cognate, and 'man and woman' is a generic pair.
The Cato partner is about ropes, not life. A 'long life' *dlh1gho- + 'life' lead (Ved. dīrghám ā́yuḥ) would need a cognate 'life' noun; líf is not cognate with ā́yus/aevum.

near_miss.lead: listing snow and frost (+wind): ON sníor ... frost ... vindar; EModIr reód ... sneachta; MW rewyd nyf; Lat nix ... pruina (ventus)
near_miss.why_not: The cognate vocabulary is solid (*sneigʷh- and *prews- in four branches), but naming snow and frost together is natural weather language, and the Irish and Welsh witnesses are late or OCR-damaged. See the search lead for the more specific eschatological-winter parallel.

near_miss.lead: binding a monster or an evildoer with fetters, *bhendh- (ON binda/band; Ved. bandh-, pāśe baddhaḥ)
near_miss.why_not: Only the root is shared. ON binda/band against bandh- with a renewed fetter noun (pāśa, rajju) is ordinary vocabulary, and the contexts differ (the proverb about Læðingr and Drómi and the binding of Loki, against magical binding in AV spells).

near_miss.lead: faðir allra guðanna ok manna ~ Hom. πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε (Il. 1.544 etc., found by search)
near_miss.why_not: Only 'father' is cognate. Snorri's wording is very likely learned (Lat. divum pater atque hominum; compare the translated Alexanders saga AM-519a-4to 14v:35 'faðir allra guða herra Jupiter'). The AV partner (pitṛbhir ... manuṣyaiḥ) is not congruent.

near_miss.lead: arming scene: hjálm setr hann sér á hǫfuð (cf. Homeric κρατὶ δ' ἐπ' ... κυνέην θῆκεν)
near_miss.why_not: The Cato partner is irrelevant. The arming type-scene uses no cognate wording (hǫfuð ~ caput, but the Greek has κράς), and Þiðreks saga is late, translated material.
Shared roots only. A sleeping giant snoring has nothing in common with sleepless nights.

near_miss.lead: no in-slab collocation (Thor's companion carrying the bag; Heimir not fleeing; the wolf growing each day; Ymir's body made into the world)
near_miss.why_not: The partners share roots only. For the Ymir passages (BS-415cb, BS-f2e83, BS-eea0d) the real parallel lies outside the slab: see the search lead.

search_lead.cognate: no lexical cognate in the head-sky slot (hauss ≠ śīrṣán; himinn ≠ dyaúḥ). The construction is parallel (ablative of the body part + the cosmic part), and the name Ymir ~ Ved. Yama, Av. Yima (*yemo- 'twin') is cognate
search_lead.argument: Snorri's cosmogony (and the older Eddic Vafþrúðnismál 21 and Grímnismál 40-41) makes the world from the body of the primordial giant: earth from flesh, sea from blood, mountains from bones, sky from skull. RV 10.90 has the same macrocosm/microcosm sacrifice (sky from the head, sun from the eye, earth from the feet). This is the well-known Ymir–Puruṣa comparison (and the 'Yemo' myth). The parallel is thematic, with no cognate wording.

search_lead.cognate: ON sníor (snjór) ~ Av. snaēžāt̰ (*sneigʷh- 'snow'). The 'winter' word is renewed (ON vetr against Av. zimō < *ǵʰeim-)
search_lead.argument: The Fimbulvetr, an eschatological winter with snow and great frosts before the world's end, is matched by Yima's evil winters (aγəm zimō, with frost and snow on the highest mountains) that will come upon the corporeal world. Both are cosmic, catastrophic winters that destroy life, and the snow verb/noun is cognate. The comparison is recalled from the literature (Fimbulwinter ~ Yima's winter), and the connection is debated; the Norse version may carry Christian-apocalyptic colouring.

error.correct_reading: járn 'iron' (dat. iarni) < PGmc *īsarną, borrowed from or shared with Celtic *īsarnom; not the PIE word for 'blood'
error.evidence: There is no standard equation of iron with *h1ésh2r̥; any link through 'blood-coloured' is speculative at best.

error.evidence: In context the three stones lie under the shoulders, under the loins and under the knee-hollows. The word is not 'land'.
The word for 'shadow' is a different word (Goth. skadus, OE sceadu).
